title: How 1 Preseason Decision Reveals the TRUTH About Cleveland's Quarterback Future
thumb_prompt: A split locker room with two jerseys hanging side by side, one number 4 and one number 2, both Browns orange and brown, under a single spotlight in a darkened facility with shadows casting doubt and uncertainty across the concrete floor
thumb_subject: Two quarterback jerseys on adjacent hangers in an NFL locker room, one bearing number 4 and the other number 2, both in Cleveland Browns colors

paragraphs.text: So Todd Monken made his call. Deshaun Watson gets the first preseason start on Saturday in Chicago. Shedeur Sanders gets the second game against Buffalo the following week. And you know what that tells us? Absolutely nothing. Because this is not a decision. This is a delay. This is a first-year head coach buying himself two more weeks before he has to pull the trigger on the most important choice of his Cleveland tenure. And honestly, I do not blame him one bit.

Monken told reporters Wednesday that he has his reasons for the order but would not elaborate. He said the competition remains ongoing. He said they will assess week by week. Translation? He does not know. And why would he? Watson has not started an NFL game since October twenty twenty four when he tore his Achilles. He sat out all of twenty twenty five rehabbing. Sanders is a fifth-round rookie who went three and four in seven starts last year with eighteen point nine quarterback rating. Neither one has earned this job.

This is Cleveland in a microcosm. A two hundred thirty million dollar mistake on one side. A developmental project on the other. And between them? The faint hope that one of them can be good enough to keep this franchise from drafting another quarterback next April. The preseason games are not about crowning a starter. They are about damage control. They are about seeing if either Watson or Sanders can prove they belong on an NFL field at all.
card_lines: Sanders fell to 5th round for a reason
Goal: avoid another QB draft in 2027

paragraphs.text: Let me take you back. Twenty twenty five training camp. The Browns had four quarterbacks. Joe Flacco. Kenny Pickett. Dillon Gabriel. Shedeur Sanders. It was chaos. Most of the first-team reps went to Pickett, who got hurt before the first preseason game. Sanders had to start that game without meaningful prep. He actually looked decent. Threw for one hundred thirty eight yards and two touchdowns against Carolina. But the process was a disaster. The Browns fumbled the competition so badly that they had no clarity heading into the season.

Now it is twenty twenty six and we are doing it again. Different names. Same script. The only difference is Monken replaced Kevin Stefanski as head coach, and Monken at least admitted back in February that he wanted the starter named by the end of spring. That did not happen. And after minicamp in June, he still would not commit. So here we are in mid-August. Training camp is nearly over. The regular season is three weeks away. And the Browns still do not have a quarterback.
card_lines: Monken wanted QB named by spring

paragraphs.text: What is wild is that Monken has been rotating Watson and Sanders with the first team all camp. One day Watson gets the starters in eleven-on-eleven. Next day Sanders gets them. Reports out of Berea say Watson has had some ugly moments. Two interceptions in back-to-back throws on the first day of camp. But he also had one of his best practices on Wednesday. Sanders has been more consistent but has not pulled away. Dillon Gabriel has actually been the steadiest of the three, which tells you how low the bar is.

Here is what Saturday will actually tell us. Not who the starter is. But whether Deshaun Watson can still play football. Because if he looks like the guy who averaged three point three yards per carry when he returned from his knee injury in twenty twenty four, if he looks like the guy who threw twelve interceptions in nineteen starts for Cleveland before the Achilles, then this is over. The two hundred thirty million dollar experiment will officially be dead. And the Browns will have no choice but to hand the keys to a twenty-four-year-old who was not good enough to go in the first four rounds.
card_lines: If he fails, Sanders wins by default

paragraphs.text: But if Watson looks competent? If he shows pocket presence, arm strength, decision-making? Then Monken has a real dilemma. Because even though Watson has been a disaster in Cleveland, he was a three-time Pro Bowler in Houston. He led the league in passing yards in twenty twenty. The talent was real. And the Browns are desperate for it to still be there. Because the alternative is riding with Sanders, and nobody in that building believes he is ready to carry this offense.

Sanders gets the second preseason game. That is interesting. Some will say Watson getting the first start means he is ahead. I do not buy it. I think Monken is giving Watson the easier assignment. Chicago is playing their backups. Buffalo will be more competitive. If Sanders handles that second game well, he might actually leap Watson. But here is the thing. Sanders threw ten interceptions in seven starts last year. His decision-making is shaky. His arm is fine but not elite. He has the pedigree from Colorado and the name recognition from his father, but this is the NFL. None of that matters.

The real wildcard is Dillon Gabriel. He was a third-round pick in twenty twenty five, higher than Sanders. He has been more consistent in camp. Reporters say he gets more attention from Monken every day. If both Watson and Sanders struggle in the preseason, do not be shocked if Gabriel sneaks into this conversation. The Browns kept four quarterbacks last year. They could do it again. And if Gabriel keeps outplaying Sanders in practice, the rookie fifth-rounder might find himself as the emergency third option instead of the backup.
card_lines: Could steal backup role from Sanders

sections.heading: THE GHOSTS OF QUARTERBACK COMPETITIONS PAST

paragraphs.text: This franchise has been wandering the quarterback desert since nineteen ninety nine. That is twenty-seven years. Twenty-seven years of training camp battles. Twenty-seven years of hoping the next guy will be the one. Think about the names. Tim Couch. Kelly Holcomb. Jeff Garcia. Derek Anderson. Brady Quinn. Colt McCoy. Brandon Weeden. Brian Hoyer. Johnny Manziel. Josh McCown. Robert Griffin the third. DeShone Kizer. Tyrod Taylor. Baker Mayfield. And now Watson and Sanders. Every single one was supposed to be the answer. None of them were.

The closest Cleveland came was Baker Mayfield. And they let him walk. Mayfield took this team to the playoffs in twenty twenty. He won a playoff game. He was not elite, but he was competent. And the Browns convinced themselves they could upgrade. So they traded for Deshaun Watson. Gave him two hundred thirty million dollars fully guaranteed. The largest guaranteed contract in NFL history at the time. And Watson has started nineteen games in three years. Nineteen. He has been hurt, suspended, ineffective. It is the worst trade in modern NFL history.

And now the Browns are trying to salvage it. That is what this preseason is really about. It is not about finding the best quarterback. It is about justifying the Watson contract. Because if they bench him for a fifth-round rookie, that is admitting defeat. That is admitting Jimmy Haslam and Andrew Berry made a catastrophic mistake. So they will give Watson every chance. They will start him in the preseason. They will start him Week One. And they will hope against hope that something clicks.

But what if it does not? What if Watson looks washed? What if Sanders is not ready? Then the Browns are staring down another lost season. They have talent on defense. Jared Verse came over in the Myles Garrett trade. Denzel Ward is still elite. The offensive line has five new starters but added real pieces. Jerry Jeudy gives them a legitimate receiver. Quinshon Judkins is a stud running back. This roster is not terrible. But none of it matters if the quarterback cannot play.

sections.heading: THE NICK CHUBB QUESTION NOBODY IS ASKING

paragraphs.text: Here is something nobody is talking about. Nick Chubb is still a free agent. He played for Houston last year after the Browns let him walk. One hundred twenty-two carries. Five hundred six yards. Three touchdowns. Not great, but he is thirty-one years old and two years removed from a gruesome knee injury. The Browns have Quinshon Judkins, who is the unquestioned starter. But behind him? Depth is thin. Judkins himself is coming off an ankle injury. Dylan Sampson is the change-of-pace guy. After that, it is a bunch of unknowns.
card_lines: Browns depth behind Judkins is thin

paragraphs.text: Multiple reports say Chubb has hinted at being open to a Browns reunion. He was at an event in Cleveland in June and said quote you never know what can happen. The fans would love it. Chubb is a franchise legend. Six thousand eight hundred forty-three yards in Cleveland. Fifty-six touchdowns. Four Pro Bowls. Only Jim Brown and Leroy Kelly have more rushing yards in franchise history. Bringing him back as a veteran third back would be a feel-good story. It would also be smart football.

But here is the problem. The Browns have not shown interest. Mary Kay Cabot reported that Cleveland is unlikely to pursue Chubb. They are going young. They are betting on Judkins and Sampson. They do not want to disrespect Chubb by bringing him back in a limited role. That is the official line. But the real reason? Money. The Browns are capped out because of the Watson contract. They cannot afford even a veteran minimum deal unless they make a corresponding move. So Chubb will probably sign somewhere else. And the Browns will regret it when Judkins gets hurt in Week Three.

That is what the Watson deal has cost this franchise. Not just the picks they gave up. Not just the nineteen mediocre starts. But the flexibility. The ability to make moves like bringing back Chubb. The ability to sign a veteran backup quarterback who could actually help. Instead, they are stuck. They are stuck with Watson. They are stuck hoping Sanders develops. They are stuck in the same cycle they have been in for twenty-seven years. And it is maddening.

So what do we watch for on Saturday? First, Watson's mobility. Can he move in the pocket? Can he escape pressure? The Achilles is a death sentence for most quarterbacks. Very few come back and look the same. If Watson is a statue back there, this is done. Second, decision-making. The interceptions have plagued him in Cleveland. If he forces balls into coverage, if he holds the ball too long, if he looks indecisive, that tells you everything. The talent does not matter if the processing is broken.

For Sanders the following week, watch his poise. Does he look overwhelmed? Does he panic when the pocket collapses? Rookie quarterbacks can get away with physical tools. But the mental side is what separates the good from the bad. Sanders has the arm. He has the bloodlines. But does he have the processing speed to succeed in the NFL? That is what Buffalo will test. And if he looks lost, the Browns are in serious trouble.

The reality is this. Neither Watson nor Sanders is the long-term answer. The Browns know it. Monken knows it. The fans know it. This is a stopgap year. The hope is that one of them can be good enough to keep Cleveland competitive while they figure out the next move. Maybe they draft a quarterback in twenty twenty seven. Maybe they trade for a veteran next offseason. But right now, this is what they have. And they have to make it work.

Monken made his decision. Watson first, Sanders second. But it is not really a decision. It is a delay. It is a hope. It is a prayer that one of these guys can be good enough to justify the last three years of misery. And if they cannot? If Saturday and the following week both end in disaster? Then the Browns are right back where they have been for nearly three decades. Searching. Hoping. Waiting for a quarterback who might never come. That is the truth this preseason will reveal. Not who the starter is. But whether this franchise has learned anything at all.
card_lines: Or doomed to repeat QB failures?
